# Maths S11 D04: What can go wrong when we collect data? Observational studies and experiments, practical faults in collecting and recording, and results that are misunderstood or misrepresented (design)

Status: Revision 3 (25 Nov 2026): preflight and fact repairs (see the final section, "Revision 3 (root, 25 November 2026)"). Revision 2 (24 Nov 2026): learning review resolved (see "Revision 2" below); not voiced. Revision 1 (24 Nov 2026): first design, written to the maths visual standard (`../maths-visual-standard.md`), `math-s11-d01.md` to `d03.md` (Revision 1, this batch), the Year 12 design that recalls this video (`math-s12-b03.md`: "Year 11: experiments and observational studies", with b03's plain meanings), the coherence audit and root's Standard rulings 1 to 99. Not voiced. Next: student learning review and Codex maths check, then voicing on the Google voice and a build on the studio kit to grade A.

Narration 5,635 characters by script (see "Narration length estimate"; Revision 2), 13 scene headings, about 504 s with holds (key notes fixed at 45 s). Nothing recorded; human listening pending.

Scope: fourth video of the Year 11 Data analysis strand, outline playlist order 64. One video for Standard 1 and Standard 2. Viewers arrive from d03's final frame. Pre-design pack: `../pre-design/maths-standard/math-s11-d04.md`. Route entry: `math-s11-d04` in `../../programme/maths-standard-route-inputs-14.json`. Site lessons: `year11/data-analysis/lesson02.sa.html` (card 06, SA 1) and `lesson09.sa.html` (card 08); experiments and observational studies are taught from the syllabus (MSY-36). Visual system: maths studio kit; the bedroom, bus, alarm clock, wall calendar, phone and exam desk plates (all existing); the study panels, allocation, fault map and headline board coded.

Owner rules applied: as d01 (header strip "DATA ANALYSIS" only; one question; one stage at a time; plain meanings; two attempts with "Pause here to answer." and 10 s countdowns; brief feedback with one crossed slip; five key notes with a framed card; everyday anchors; no people, hands or faces; Australian spelling; no em dashes).

Syllabus content point (Mathematics Standard 11-12 (2024), Year 11, Data analysis, "Population and sample", common to Standard 1 and Standard 2), quoted from `../../programme/maths-standard-route-inputs-14.json`:

- `ci4c7cc505`: "Describe the potential faults in the design and practicalities of a data collection process by considering survey design, experiments and observational studies, and misunderstandings and misrepresentations"

Source: https://curriculum.nsw.edu.au/learning-areas/mathematics/mathematics-standard-11-12-2024/content/year-11/fa4de413b8

**Boundary:** starts from d03's final frame exactly (the bedroom `ms12-bedroom-furniture-v1.png`, about 900 px wide, at the left with the white headline card "Phones in bedrooms steal 2 hours of sleep!"; at the right the 20 blue tokens in two olive-labelled groups "phone in bedroom: 12" and "elsewhere: 8"; chips "What could go wrong?", "Next: faults in data collection" and "?"). Recalls d01 (question faults), d02 (bias; honest reporting) and d03 (random; self-selected; representative) in grey chips. Teaches: observational studies and controlled experiments; faults in each; practical faults; survey design faults; misunderstandings and misrepresentations. Not taught: data types (d05); misleading graphs (d10).

## Revision 2: learning review resolved (24 Nov 2026)

Source review: `../checks/m-s11-d04-learning-review.md`; resolution record `../checks/m-s11-d-learning-review-resolution.md`.

- **D04-2H (note): applied.** Scene 5 now says "Our survey found a smaller difference, and only on average." (d10 and d14 report about 1.5 hours).
- **D04-A1PIC (note): applied.** Attempt 1's picture slot is left to the card: the food truck plate is a different place from a school canteen, and no canteen plate exists. The Assets section records the food truck as inspected but not used.
- Narration 5,647 characters (Revision 1: 5,643); about 505 s with holds, under the 570 s cap. Both attempts still end "Pause here to answer."; feedback about 24.6 s and 22.9 s. No em dash. Joins unchanged.

## Decisions

- **Anchor: the headline (d03's frame).** "Phones in bedrooms steal 2 hours of sleep!" is wrong in three ways the video unpicks: it claims a cause from watching, it generalises from 20 students, and its "2 hours" is not what the survey found. The headline is rewritten in scene 5.
- **Year 12 b03's words, word for word.** Observational study: "just watching what happens". Controlled experiment: "change one thing on purpose and keep everything else the same". b03 recalls them in a grey chip.
- **The hidden factor is shown, not named as jargon.** The bus students wake early, and (in this example) more of them charge their phones in their bedrooms, so the bedroom group sleeps less partly because of the bus. "Confounding" is not used; the phrase is "something else could explain the difference".
- **The experiment that could show cause.** 40 volunteers; a random draw puts 20 in "phone charges in the kitchen for two weeks" and 20 in "usual"; random allocation spreads the bus students and everything else across both groups. Its own faults: people sneaking phones back, knowing they're watched, two weeks may be too short, volunteers may not represent Year 11, and letting people pick their own group.
- **Practical faults as a pipeline (recurring model).** Question, people, method, recording, claim: the stages where faults drop as pins. This becomes the memory aid ("Check the question, the people, the method, the recording and the claim").
- **Plain meanings at first use.** Observational study; controlled experiment (both as above); non-response ("people who were chosen but didn't answer"); misrepresentation ("presenting results so they seem to show more than they do").
- **Simulations (standard item 3).**
  1. **Hidden-factor reveal** (scene 2): the 12 bedroom tokens turn over to show bus badges on 5 of them (against 1 of the 8 elsewhere; example), and a faint arrow from the bus to "less sleep" appears beside the phone arrow.
  2. **Random allocation** (scene 3): 40 volunteer tokens (6 with bus badges) shuffle and split 20 and 20 by a random draw; a counter shows the bus badges landing 3 and 3; then a "choose your own group" version lands 6 and 0.
  3. **Fault map** (scenes 4, 5): five pipeline stages; fault pins drop with short labels; a "trust" meter falls with each pin and rises as fixes are applied.
- **Colour roles (strand, fixed).** As d01: values blue; counts olive; mean teal; median and quartiles violet; spread and fences amber; survey wording and steps violet labels; answer green; mistake red. Here: the hidden factor (bus badges) amber-outlined as in d02 and d03.
- **Large type, handwritten voice.** Labels 40 px; working 52 px; nothing below 26 px; all text above y = 950. Hand tags: "just watching", "something else?", "change one thing on purpose", "random groups", "chose their own group", "who didn't answer?", "75 hours?", "one school, one night", "12 of 20", "tended to, not caused". At most two live at once.
- **Stage changes (standard item 2).** The headline (1); the observational panel and hidden factor (2); the experiment panel and allocation (3); the fault map, practical faults (4); the headline board (5); the fault map completed with fixes (6); framed card (7); question cards (8 to 11); the record sheet (12); key notes (13).
- **Worked examples (g01 order).** Scene 5: the headline struck word by word; rewrite "In our sample of 20 Year 11 students, those who charged phones in their bedrooms tended to report less sleep. This does not show the phone caused it." (framed green).
- **Memory aid.** Framed card: "Check the question, the people, the method, the recording and the claim." Key line: "An experiment changes one thing on purpose; an observational study just watches. Only a fair experiment can show cause."
- **Attempts.** A1 (pack question 1): observational; another explanation; crossed "(a) experiment, because they measured marks" (caption "nothing was changed on purpose"). A2 (pack question 2): non-response and timing; crossed "200 replies is plenty" (caption "2% chose to reply").
- **Mistake scene:** none separate. Cause from watching (2, 5, A1); self-chosen groups (3); non-response (4, A2); generalising (5); a percentage of a tiny sample (5).
- **Cause chain taught, in order:** (1) an observational study only watches, so the groups can differ in other ways that also affect the result, and those other differences could explain it (2); (2) an experiment changes one thing on purpose and uses random groups, so other differences are spread evenly and a difference in results can be put down to the change (3); (3) practical faults (missing replies, guessed or rounded answers, typing errors, an unusual week) change the data before anyone analyses it (4); (4) a claim can say more than the data show (cause, everyone, a bigger number), so the conclusion must match the method and the sample (5).
- **Entry knowledge (route):** math-s11-d01 (question faults), d02 (bias; reporting), d03 (random; self-selected; representative). Recalled in grey chips.
- **Site notes.** MSY-36 (experiments, observational studies and misrepresentation are not taught).
- **Handoff (to math-s11-d05, types of data).** Scene 12: board clear; the exam desk `ma12-exam-desk-v1.png` (about 1,000 px wide) with a coded record sheet over the notebook (blue, 32 px rows, 5 visible rows of 20): columns "Sleep (h)", "Screens in bedroom", "Phone charges", "How rested?", "Gets to school"; first row "7.5 | 2 | bedroom | a little | bus"; chips "Numbers or words?", "Next: types of data" and "?". d05 opens on this frame.
- **Legacy logic ported:** none.
- **Author notes (not learner copy):**
  (a) Hidden factor (example): of the 6 bus students in the sample, 5 charge phones in their bedrooms and 1 elsewhere (bedroom group 12 = 5 bus + 7 nearby; elsewhere 8 = 1 bus + 7 nearby). Labelled "example".
  (b) Allocation: 40 volunteers with 6 bus badges; the seeded random split gives 3 and 3; the self-chosen version 6 and 0 (example).
  (c) 12 ÷ 20 = 60%; 15 of 20 returned = 75% (5 missing); 200 ÷ 10 000 = 2%.
  (d) "2 hours" in the headline is not supported: the sample's medians later differ by 1.25 h (d17: 6.75 and 8); not said here, only that "the survey didn't find two hours for everyone".

Main question: *"Phones in bedrooms steal 2 hours of sleep!" Can our survey show that? What can go wrong when we collect data?*

Stops after: observational studies and experiments; practical faults; misunderstandings and misrepresentations.

teaching.task: # Maths S11 D04: What can go wrong when we collect data? Observational studies and experiments, practical faults in collecting and recording, and results that are misunderstood or misrepresented (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: Look at how our data were collected. We didn't tell anyone where to charge their phone. We just asked. That's an observational study, just watching what happens. Observational studies are useful, but they have a big weakness. The two groups can differ in other ways too. Remember the early bus? In our sample, five of the six bus students charge their phones in their bedrooms. Bus students get up earlier. So the bedroom group might sleep less because of the bus, not the phone. Something else could explain the difference. That's why an observational study can show that two things happen together, but it can't show that one causes the other. To test whether the phone itself makes a difference, you'd run a controlled experiment. That means you change one thing on purpose, and keep everything else the same. Take forty volunteers. A random draw puts twenty of them in a group whose phones charge in the kitchen for two weeks, and the other twenty carry on as usual. The random draw is the key. It spreads the bus students, and everything else, across both groups, three bus students in each. If the kitchen group then sleeps more, the phone is the likely reason. Experiments have faults too. If people choose their own group, all six bus students might end up together. People might sneak their phones back, or sleep differently because they know they're being watched. And two weeks might be too short, or forty volunteers might not represent Year 11. Now the practical side. Picture the whole process as a pipeline, from the question, to the people, to the method, to the recording, to the claim. Faults can creep in at every stage. The question might be unclear, like our old overlapping buttons. Some people chosen for the sample might not reply. If five of our twenty don't answer, and they're the ones who slept least, the results look better than they are. People guess and round. Ask about sleep, and lots of answers come back as whole hours. Someone might type seven point five as seventy-five, and suddenly a student slept seventy-five hours. And timing matters. A survey in exam week, or after a long weekend, describes that week, not a normal one. The fix is to plan for each stage, follow up the people who didn't reply, and check the data before you use it.

teaching.openingDecision: Visual: opens on d03's final frame exactly. On "Our survey's in" the "Next" chips fade; the two token groups pulse olive. On "reported less sleep" a small olive bar pair under the tokens, the bedroom bar slightly shorter (no numbers). On "this headline" the headline card enlarges (52 px). teaching.understandingCheck: Your turn. A school finds that students who eat breakfast at the school canteen get higher marks, and claims that canteen breakfasts raise marks. Is this an experiment, or an observational study? Then give one reason the claim may be wrong. Pause here to answer. Last one. A phone company texts ten thousand customers at two in the morning. Rate our network from one to ten. Two hundred reply. Describe two faults in this data collection. Pause here to answer.

## Decisions

- **Anchor: the headline (d03's frame).** "Phones in bedrooms steal 2 hours of sleep!" is wrong in three ways the video unpicks: it claims a cause from watching, it generalises from 20 students, and its "2 hours" is not what the survey found. The headline is rewritten in scene 5.
- **Year 12 b03's words, word for word.** Observational study: "just watching what happens". Controlled experiment: "change one thing on purpose and keep everything else the same". b03 recalls them in a grey chip.
- **The hidden factor is shown, not named as jargon.** The bus students wake early, and (in this example) more of them charge their phones in their bedrooms, so the bedroom group sleeps less partly because of the bus. "Confounding" is not used; the phrase is "something else could explain the difference".
- **The experiment that could show cause.** 40 volunteers; a random draw puts 20 in "phone charges in the kitchen for two weeks" and 20 in "usual"; random allocation spreads the bus students and everything else across both groups. Its own faults: people sneaking phones back, knowing they're watched, two weeks may be too short, volunteers may not represent Year 11, and letting people pick their own group.
- **Practical faults as a pipeline (recurring model).** Question, people, method, recording, claim: the stages where faults drop as pins. This becomes the memory aid ("Check the question, the people, the method, the recording and the claim").
- **Plain meanings at first use.** Observational study; controlled experiment (both as above); non-response ("people who were chosen but didn't answer"); misrepresentation ("presenting results so they seem to show more than they do").
- **Simulations (standard item 3).**
  1. **Hidden-factor reveal** (scene 2): the 12 bedroom tokens turn over to show bus badges on 5 of them (against 1 of the 8 elsewhere; example), and a faint arrow from the bus to "less sleep" appears beside the phone arrow.
  2. **Random allocation** (scene 3): 40 volunteer tokens (6 with bus badges) shuffle and split 20 and 20 by a random draw; a counter shows the bus badges landing 3 and 3; then a "choose your own group" version lands 6 and 0.
  3. **Fault map** (scenes 4, 5): five pipeline stages; fault pins drop with short labels; a "trust" meter falls with each pin and rises as fixes are applied.
- **Colour roles (strand, fixed).** As d01: values blue; counts olive; mean teal; median and quartiles violet; spread and fences amber; survey wording and steps violet labels; answer green; mistake red. Here: the hidden factor (bus badges) amber-outlined as in d02 and d03.
- **Large type, handwritten voice.** Labels 40 px; working 52 px; nothing below 26 px; all text above y = 950. Hand tags: "just watching", "something else?", "change one thing on purpose", "random groups", "chose their own group", "who didn't answer?", "75 hours?", "one school, one night", "12 of 20", "tended to, not caused". At most two live at once.
- **Stage changes (standard item 2).** The headline (1); the observational panel and hidden factor (2); the experiment panel and allocation (3); the fault map, practical faults (4); the headline board (5); the fault map completed with fixes (6); framed card (7); question cards (8 to 11); the record sheet (12); key notes (13).
- **Worked examples (g01 order).** Scene 5: the headline struck word by word; rewrite "In our sample of 20 Year 11 students, those who charged phones in their bedrooms tended to report less sleep. This does not show the phone caused it." (framed green).
- **Memory aid.** Framed card: "Check the question, the people, the method, the recording and the claim." Key line: "An experiment changes one thing on purpose; an observational study just watches. Only a fair experiment can show cause."
- **Attempts.** A1 (pack question 1): observational; another explanation; crossed "(a) experiment, because they measured marks" (caption "nothing was changed on purpose"). A2 (pack question 2): non-response and timing; crossed "200 replies is plenty" (caption "2% chose to reply").
- **Mistake scene:** none separate. Cause from watching (2, 5, A1); self-chosen groups (3); non-response (4, A2); generalising (5); a percentage of a tiny sample (5).
- **Cause chain taught, in order:** (1) an observational study only watches, so the groups can differ in other ways that also affect the result, and those other differences could explain it (2); (2) an experiment changes one thing on purpose and uses random groups, so other differences are spread evenly and a difference in results can be put down to the change (3); (3) practical faults (missing replies, guessed or rounded answers, typing errors, an unusual week) change the data before anyone analyses it (4); (4) a claim can say more than the data show (cause, everyone, a bigger number), so the conclusion must match the method and the sample (5).
- **Entry knowledge (route):** math-s11-d01 (question faults), d02 (bias; reporting), d03 (random; self-selected; representative). Recalled in grey chips.
- **Site notes.** MSY-36 (experiments, observational studies and misrepresentation are not taught).
- **Handoff (to math-s11-d05, types of data).** Scene 12: board clear; the exam desk `ma12-exam-desk-v1.png` (about 1,000 px wide) with a coded record sheet over the notebook (blue, 32 px rows, 5 visible rows of 20): columns "Sleep (h)", "Screens in bedroom", "Phone charges", "How rested?", "Gets to school"; first row "7.5 | 2 | bedroom | a little | bus"; chips "Numbers or words?", "Next: types of data" and "?". d05 opens on this frame.
- **Legacy logic ported:** none.
- **Author notes (not learner copy):**
  (a) Hidden factor (example): of the 6 bus students in the sample, 5 charge phones in their bedrooms and 1 elsewhere (bedroom group 12 = 5 bus + 7 nearby; elsewhere 8 = 1 bus + 7 nearby). Labelled "example".
  (b) Allocation: 40 volunteers with 6 bus badges; the seeded random split gives 3 and 3; the self-chosen version 6 and 0 (example).
  (c) 12 ÷ 20 = 60%; 15 of 20 returned = 75% (5 missing); 200 ÷ 10 000 = 2%.
  (d) "2 hours" in the headline is not supported: the sample's medians later differ by 1.25 h (d17: 6.75 and 8); not said here, only that "the survey didn't find two hours for everyone".

scenes.teachingReason: Look at how our data were collected. We didn't tell anyone where to charge their phone. We just asked. That's an observational study, just watching what happens. Observational studies are useful, but they have a big weakness. The two groups can differ in other ways too. Remember the early bus? In our sample, five of the six bus students charge their phones in their bedrooms. Bus students get up earlier. So the bedroom group might sleep less because of the bus, not the phone. Something else could explain the difference. That's why an observational study can show that two things happen together, but it can't show that one causes the other.

scenes.teachingReason: To test whether the phone itself makes a difference, you'd run a controlled experiment. That means you change one thing on purpose, and keep everything else the same. Take forty volunteers. A random draw puts twenty of them in a group whose phones charge in the kitchen for two weeks, and the other twenty carry on as usual. The random draw is the key. It spreads the bus students, and everything else, across both groups, three bus students in each. If the kitchen group then sleeps more, the phone is the likely reason. Experiments have faults too. If people choose their own group, all six bus students might end up together. People might sneak their phones back, or sleep differently because they know they're being watched. And two weeks might be too short, or forty volunteers might not represent Year 11.

scenes.teachingReason: Now the practical side. Picture the whole process as a pipeline, from the question, to the people, to the method, to the recording, to the claim. Faults can creep in at every stage. The question might be unclear, like our old overlapping buttons. Some people chosen for the sample might not reply. If five of our twenty don't answer, and they're the ones who slept least, the results look better than they are. People guess and round. Ask about sleep, and lots of answers come back as whole hours. Someone might type seven point five as seventy-five, and suddenly a student slept seventy-five hours. And timing matters. A survey in exam week, or after a long weekend, describes that week, not a normal one. The fix is to plan for each stage, follow up the people who didn't reply, and check the data before you use it.

scenes.teachingReason: The last stage is the claim, and this is where the headline goes wrong. A misrepresentation presents results so they seem to show more than they do. Steal says the phone causes it, but ours was an observational study. Phones in bedrooms suggests every teenager, but we asked twenty students at one school, on one night. Our survey found a smaller difference, and only on average. Percentages can mislead too. Sixty per cent of students sleep with their phone sounds huge, but it's twelve out of twenty. Misunderstandings happen on the other side, when people read a result, or a question, differently from what was meant. Hours slept might be read as hours in bed. Here's an honest version. In our sample of twenty Year 11 students, those who charged their phones in their bedrooms tended to report less sleep. That doesn't show the phone caused it.

scenes.teachingReason: So whenever you judge a data collection, walk the pipeline. Is the question clear? Did the right people answer, and did enough of them reply? Was it an experiment or an observational study, and does the claim match? Were the answers recorded and checked? And does the claim stay inside what the sample and method can show? Every yes makes the results easier to trust.

scenes.teachingReason: Nobody was told to eat breakfast there. The school just recorded what happened, so it's an observational study. The claim may be wrong because something else could explain both. Students who arrive early for breakfast might be more organised, or get more sleep. Calling it an experiment because marks were measured is the slip.

scenes.teachingReason: First, non-response. Only two hundred of ten thousand replied, two per cent, and they chose to, so the very happy or very annoyed are over-represented. Second, timing. A text at two in the morning misses or wakes most customers, so night owls answer most. Saying two hundred replies is plenty is the slip.

Row "2: timing; 2 am misses most customers" (framed green). On "slip" a red slip "200 replies is plenty" writes and is crossed (caption "2% chose to reply"). Hold about 1 s.
